items.title: Boundary versus ownership
items.scenario: A municipal flood-warning service consumes a commercial rainfall feed. The supplier controls its infrastructure. The warning authority remains accountable for issuing timely warnings when the feed is delayed.
items.question: How should the supplier be represented?

choices.A: As a fixed environmental assumption until the supplier contract is renegotiated.
choices.B: Inside the authority's boundary because accountability implies control of all supporting components.
choices.C: Outside the architecture because its implementation cannot be changed by the authority.
choices.D: Outside the system-of-interest boundary, with an explicit operational dependency and an owned degraded-service response.

items.title: Conflicting outcomes
items.scenario: Airport operations wants shorter gate turnaround; maintenance wants enough inspection time; crews report increasing last-minute changes. The team proposes automation of the inspection signoff. No causal study is available.
items.question: Which pair of actions is justified before committing to that automation?

choices.A: Define the competing outcomes and the conditions under which each must be protected.
choices.B: Assign the delay to maintenance because it owns the signoff.
choices.C: Use the fastest observed turnaround as the acceptance threshold.
choices.D: Trace late changes and inspection decisions across responsible roles.

items.title: End of service
items.scenario: A sensor network stores configuration keys in modules expected to remain installed for fifteen years. The design review covers commissioning and operation but not replacement or retirement.
items.question: Which issues belong in the lifecycle review?

choices.A: Whether every module should be physically destroyed on replacement.
choices.B: Who maintains compatibility and spares when the supplier ends support.
choices.C: How replacement modules acquire the authorized configuration.
choices.D: How retired modules lose credentials and retained sensitive data.

items.title: Reliability across a mission
items.scenario: Two alternatives have the same measured failure frequency during operation. One restores within minutes after a fault; the other requires a specialist visit. Missions are daily and unattended sites have limited access.
items.question: What conclusion follows?

choices.A: Equal failure frequency establishes equal operational availability.
choices.B: Restoration time and access arrangements must be included before comparing mission availability and lifecycle effort.
choices.C: Availability cannot be studied until a complete long-term field trial has finished.
choices.D: The faster-restoring alternative is preferable regardless of acquisition and mission effects.

items.title: A shared event in a tree
items.scenario: A fault tree is (A AND B) OR (A AND C). Event A represents the same loss of a shared supply wherever it appears.
items.question: Which minimal cut sets follow from that Boolean model?

choices.A: {A,B,C} only.
choices.B: Two separate independent copies of A, one in each branch.
choices.C: {A} and {B,C}.
choices.D: {A,B} and {A,C}.

items.title: A warning that causes more work
items.scenario: An alarm threshold is lowered. Detection rises, but operators receive many more alarms and begin delaying acknowledgment. Reported unresolved incidents also rise.
items.question: Which next model is most useful?

choices.A: A feedback model connecting alarm load, attention, acknowledgment, escalation and unresolved events.
choices.B: A ranking of operators by acknowledgment time.
choices.C: A detector-only ROC curve with an increased penalty for missed events.
choices.D: A human-response model using the old acknowledgment time as a constant.

items.title: Zero observed failures
items.scenario: An engineer tests twenty identical units for one hour each and observes no failures. The report claims the system failure probability is zero.
items.question: Which response is most appropriate?

choices.A: Pool the twenty units as a single unit tested for twenty consecutive hours without checking assumptions.
choices.B: State the observed exposure and zero events, then use an explicitly justified statistical model and uncertainty if estimating reliability.
choices.C: Declare the test inconclusive and discard the observations.
choices.D: Use one failure divided by exposure as the exact failure probability.

items.title: Coverage with an unrealistic assumption
items.scenario: A formal check proves that every accepted request is eventually served under an assumption that the shared resource is continuously available. Deployed operation allows outages and bounded recovery.
items.question: Which next step best strengthens the evidence?

choices.A: Report the proof as conditional, assess the environment assumption, and analyze request behavior during outage and recovery.
choices.B: Remove the availability assumption and call the resulting timeout a requirement defect.
choices.C: Increase the proof bound while leaving the environment assumption unchanged.
choices.D: Replace the proof with line coverage because the deployed environment is uncertain.

items.title: Decomposition loses a condition
items.scenario: The parent requires emergency shutdown on loss of either pressure sensing or temperature sensing. Two children require a diagnostic on pressure loss and a diagnostic on temperature loss. The allocation matrix links both children to the parent.
items.question: What remains missing?

choices.A: A third sensor is needed to satisfy the parent.
choices.B: The two links establish complete decomposition because each input is represented.
choices.C: The children must use identical wording to the parent.
choices.D: The required shutdown response and its connection to either diagnostic need explicit treatment.

items.title: Resolving conflicting authorities
items.scenario: A signed contract requires a maximum mass of 40 kg. A later meeting note proposes 45 kg to improve endurance but contains no approval. The team is preparing a design trade.
items.question: Which treatment preserves the decision basis?

choices.A: Stop all concept work until the contract is formally changed.
choices.B: Keep 40 kg as the current obligation, record 45 kg as a proposed change, and show the trade consequence and needed disposition.
choices.C: Use 45 kg because it is the latest statement.
choices.D: Average the two values to avoid bias toward either stakeholder.

items.title: Mars Climate Orbiter: a contract existed
items.scenario: The 1999 Mars Climate Orbiter investigation reports that a ground software interface specified metric impulse data, while a producer supplied English-unit data. The report also identifies verification and communication weaknesses.
items.question: Which action best transfers this lesson to a new project?

choices.A: Add unit labels to the interface document and consider the problem resolved.
choices.B: Require one organization to write every component to remove organizational interfaces.
choices.C: Convert every engineering quantity to a single storage type.
choices.D: Make interface semantics executable at producer/consumer boundaries and verify representative exchanged data with clear ownership.

items.title: Ownership at an interface
items.scenario: A sensor supplier guarantees nominal one-second updates. The controller designer assumes the latest value is usable for five seconds. Neither defines timestamps, loss detection or clock alignment.
items.question: Which clarification has the highest immediate value?

choices.A: The validity/age contract, clock reference, guaranteed update bounds and responsibilities when those conditions are violated.
choices.B: Whether the supplier uses UDP or TCP internally.
choices.C: The exact color of the stale-data indicator.
choices.D: Whether five seconds is a common industry setting.

items.title: A reversible trial
items.scenario: Two scheduling policies meet hard constraints in preliminary analysis. A can be trialed at one site with rapid rollback; B requires a year-long infrastructure change. Demand forecasts are uncertain and likely to change within six months.
items.question: Which factor belongs in the decision?

choices.A: The number of requirements each option references.
choices.B: The option value of reversible learning, alongside expected performance and implementation effects.
choices.C: A rule that the smallest change should always be selected.
choices.D: A preference for B because it demonstrates long-term commitment.

items.title: Build, buy and the supporting system
items.scenario: A defense logistics team can buy a sensor that meets laboratory accuracy requirements. Field repair, export/access constraints, supply continuity and integration with existing maintenance records remain unresolved.
items.question: What should a build/buy comparison include?

choices.A: Only components designed by the program because external products cannot be controlled.
choices.B: The sensor plus integration, support, supply and operational constraints, with uncertainties and owners.
choices.C: Total project cost with all unknowns assigned the same contingency percentage.
choices.D: The sensing function and its measured accuracy only.

items.title: An estimate becomes a fact

choices.B: Delete every result calculated using the assumed value.
choices.C: Increase the value until the conclusion becomes conservative.
choices.D: Retain the value but restore its assumption status and trace its effect on conclusions.

items.title: US Airways 1549: decision time in a simulation
items.scenario: The NTSB's report on the 2009 US Airways 1549 accident distinguishes immediate-return simulator attempts from scenarios including crew decision time. An immediate turn toward an airport does not represent the same starting conditions as the actual crew's situation.
items.question: What is the strongest transferable lesson?

choices.A: Alternative assessment must include information, recognition and decision delays available at the actual decision point.
choices.B: A successful simulator trajectory establishes that the crew should have selected it.
choices.C: Human decision time should be removed when evaluating aircraft performance.
choices.D: A failed delayed attempt proves no aircraft could have returned under any conditions.

items.title: Columbia: routine success and unresolved evidence
items.scenario: The 2003 Columbia Accident Investigation Board analyzes both physical damage mechanisms and organizational practices. A contemporary team argues that a recurring anomaly is acceptable because previous missions succeeded.
items.question: What should a review require?

choices.B: A ban on using operational history in risk assessment.
choices.C: A count of successful missions as a direct estimate that the anomaly cannot cause loss.
choices.D: A requirement that the subsystem owner make the final decision without cross-program review.

choices.C: Exercised scenarios connecting delivery shortfalls to decision authority, available reserves and operational changes.

items.title: Reporting disagreement
items.scenario: Two reviewers disagree about whether an old environmental test covers a revised connector. One cites unchanged materials; the other cites a changed seal geometry. A report must be delivered today.
items.question: Which report is most useful?

choices.A: Report disagreement, the evidence supporting each position, the geometry-dependent question and the decision or test needed to resolve it.
choices.B: Choose the senior reviewer's conclusion and omit the disagreement.
choices.C: Present both conclusions as equally valid without identifying the unresolved mechanism.
choices.D: Average the two reviewer ratings and report the resulting confidence.

items.title: Choosing a useful view

items.title: TCP: acknowledgment at the right layer
items.scenario: RFC 793 (1981) explains that TCP acknowledgment means the receiving TCP has taken responsibility for data, not necessarily that it has been delivered to the end user. A system logs TCP acknowledgment as proof that a remote operator acted.
items.question: What should the review conclude?

choices.A: Replacing TCP with a newer transport protocol resolves the semantic gap.
choices.B: TCP acknowledgments are unreliable and should not be recorded.
choices.C: The log supports transport-level receipt but not operator action; the application/workflow needs its own relevant acknowledgment evidence.
choices.D: The operator action is established whenever both endpoints use TCP.

items.title: DNS: a historical design trade
items.scenario: RFC 1034 (1987) describes distributed maintenance and caching, including a trade among acquisition cost, update speed and cache accuracy. A team proposes a very long cache lifetime to reduce server load for rapidly changing control data.
items.question: What transfers from the source?

choices.A: A long lifetime is correct because the original design favored caching.
choices.B: The trade must be evaluated against this application's update and stale-data consequences; the historical mechanism does not supply its acceptance limits.
choices.C: Caching should be avoided whenever data can change.
choices.D: A cache hit demonstrates that the value is current.

choices.B: The supplier's event count, because no data is lost.

items.title: A rejected alternative becomes relevant
items.scenario: A system chose a wired sensor because radio coverage was poor at remote sites. The new deployment is indoors with existing radio infrastructure, but battery replacement staffing is limited.
items.question: What should the concept review do?

choices.A: Delete the previous decision record to avoid confusing reviewers.
choices.B: Reuse the old decision because its documented rationale makes it authoritative in every deployment.
choices.C: Select radio because the original objection is absent.
choices.D: Reopen the alternative against the new context, retaining the old rationale and examining new support constraints.
